Micro-aeration strategy for improved biogas yield and in-situ hydrogen 
sulfide mitigation during high-solids co-digestion of poultry litter
Bhavya Karumanchi a,b,c, Sameena Begum a,c, Gangagni Rao Anupoju a,c,*

Biplob Kumar Pramanik b

G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T

A B S T R A C T
High-solids anaerobic digestion sustainably converts organic waste into methane-rich biogas and nutrient-rich 
biomanure, offering dual benefits. This study assessed poultry litter (PL) digestion at 10 %, 30 %, and 60 % 
total solids (TS) under three setups: (i) PL alone, (ii) co-digestion with food waste hydrolysate (PL + FH) to 
improve carbon/nitrogen (C/N) ratio, and (iii) in situ desulfurization (St-PL) using sulfur-oxidizing bacteria 
(SOB) with micro-aeration to reduce H2S. The highest biogas yields were obtained at 30 % TS: 12.4 L (PL + FH), 
9.9 L (PL), and 8.9 L (St-PL). Methane content was highest in St-PL (68 %) with H2S removal of 80–92 %. 
However, slight sulfate accumulation was detected in the digestate, attributed to the metabolic activity of sulfur 
oxidizing bacteria (SOB). Microbial analysis revealed the dominance of Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, Methanosaeta, 
and Methanobacterium. This study demonstrates a scalable strategy in which micro-aeration combined with SOB 
enhanced methane yield and biogas quality while effectively mitigating H2S during high-solids poultry litter 
digestion.

1. Introduction
The accumulation of poultry litter, a major by-product of the poultry 
industry, poses significant environmental challenges due to its high ni­
trogen content which leads to ammonia emissions, nutrient leaching and 
groundwater pollution, the release of greenhouse gases (GHGs), and the 
spread of pathogens. It is estimated that in 2024, the global chicken 
meat production was ~103,046 tons, which is associated with the 
generation of approximately 68 billion tons of poultry waste annually 
(Coˆelho et al., 2025). Over the past five decades, the production of 
poultry litter (PL) has increased by an average of 5 % per annum, along 
with other associated wastes, including droppings; bedding materials 
such as straw, sawdust, wood shavings, and rice hulls; hatchery waste; 
feathers; and processing wastewater generated during and after the 
production period (Beausang et al., 2020; Moreki & Keaikitse, 2013; 
Mottet & Tempio, 2017).
These waste materials possess properties that can substantially 
exacerbate pollution, leading to health hazards. Current treatment 
methods for poultry litter include biological, physico-chemical and 
thermal methods. However, most of these approaches are not cost- 
effective and are complex to implement, whereas biological treatment 
through the anaerobic digestion (AD) approach offers the dual benefit of 
cost-effectiveness and the generation of biogas and biomanure, 
contributing to the circular bioeconomy. AD is widely utilised for the 
treatment of a diversity of organic wastes, including cattle and pig 
manure, which share similar characteristics with poultry litter, partic­
ularly the hazardous emissions of H2S and ammonia (NH3). These wastes 
cause contamination through pathogens, odours, and pests, while 
manure facilities emit CO2, CH4, and N2O, contributing to global 
warming. The sulfur content in poultry litter hinders the metabolism and 
growth of methanogenic archaea by promoting toxic sulfide production 
and by allowing sulfur-reducing bacteria (SRB) to compete for essential 
substrates. Poultry farms supplement feeds with sulfur-containing 
amino acids like methionine and cysteine, as chicks cannot synthesize 
them; these are essential for protein synthesis, feather growth, and 
improved egg production (Capson-Tojo et al., 2017). PL, rich in sulfur 
amino acids and organics, generates sulfur by-products during AD, 
creating microbial competition that lowers biogas yield and methane 
production (Mahdy et al., 2020).
Based on the total solids (TS) content of the feedstock, AD can be 
categorised into three types; wet AD, semi-dry AD, and dry AD or solid- 
state AD (Arelli et al., 2021). Compared to wet AD (TS 10 %), semi-dry 
AD (15–20 %), dry or solid-state AD (TS > 20 %) has recently gained 
significant research attention due to its various benefits including 
reduced water demand, higher methane yield, and less digestate gen­
eration. Although AD is typically divided into four phases, all reactions 
occur simultaneously and are highly interdependent. Each phase is 
associated with a distinct microbial community with diverse microbial 
consortia. The solid-state anaerobic digestion (SSAD) method was 
initially employed for treating the organic fraction of municipal solid 
waste (Li et al., 2011; Begum et al., 2024). However, it has recently been 
proposed for the treatment of agricultural crop residues, livestock, and 
poultry waste, often in combination with energy crops, to produce a 
stable digestate in solid phase (Chiumenti et al., 2018). Despite its 
promise, SSAD technology requires further development and investi­
gation to reach maturity and expand the range of substrates it can 
effectively process.
The digestibility of carbon and nitrogen sources is critical in deter­
mining the optimum C/N ratio for AD. PL typically has low C/N ratio, 
ranging from 7 to 10, which is suboptimal for the AD process. However, 
Kirchmann & Witter (1992) observed that the C/N ratio increases during 
the AD of PL in uncovered containers, likely due to preferential loss of 
carbon (as CO2) relative to nitrogen under those conditions. Under­
standing the roles of anaerobic bacteria such as hydrolytic, acidogenic, 
acetogenic and syntrophic bacteria and methanogenic archaea is critical 
for monitoring the AD process, avoiding disruptions, and improving the 
efficiency of biogas reactors (Wang et al., 2018). To enhance methane 
production, it is essential to investigate the structure and interactions 
between microbial communities and the operating conditions under 
which they function (Ziganshina et al., 2022; Kang et al., 2019).
This study examined the AD of PL at different solid concentrations 
(10 %, 30 %, and 60 %), incorporating co-digestion with food waste 
hydrolysate (FH) to optimise the C/N ratio, and introducing sulfur- 
oxidizing bacteria (SOB) with micro-aeration for in situ desulfuriza­
tion and methane yield enhancement. The results provide a strong 
foundation for advancing SSAD of PL. Uniquely, this work integrates 
high-solids AD with FH co-digestion, SOB-mediated H2S removal, and 
micro-aeration in a single system, coupled with microbial community 
profiling using high-throughput sequencing (454 pyrosequencing and 
Illumina). This approach achieves enhanced methane yield, maximum 
H2S removal efficiency, and offers the first comprehensive insight into 
microbial diversity and its role in high-solids PL digestion for biofuel 
production.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Feedstock procurement and sample preparation
Approximately 10 kg of PL was collected from a poultry farm from 
the outskirts of Hyderabad city in Telangana State, India. The litter was 
placed in a sealed bag and transported to the laboratory within a few 
hours of collection. The PL comprised of cage litter, which included 
bedding material such as straw, wood shavings, and sawdust, along with 
poultry droppings. The collected PL was ground to ensure homogeneity 
and stored in a refrigerator at 4 ◦C for subsequent biomethanation ex­
periments. The raw PL was initially characterized for parameters such as 
TS and VS using standard methods as described in APHA. For this, 10 % 
TS containing PL slurry was prepared with deionized (DI) water, and 
was used for all subsequent characterization of raw PL. Prior to the 
experiments, PL slurry of 10 % TS, 30 % TS, and 60 % TS was prepared 
12 h in advance, adjusted to meet the TS requirements of the study, and 
its pH was acclimatised by adding dilute hydrochloric acid from an 
initial value of 7.9 to an optimal 7 for AD.
The co-substrate used in the experiments was food waste hydrolysate 
(FH), which served as a carbon source to dilute the PL as well as to adjust 
pH. Food waste (FW) is rich in carbon (C), making FH an effective means 
of balancing the C/N ratio of PL, which is 8.9. Approximately 5 kg of 
coarsely ground FW was collected from a biogas plant operated in CSIR- 
IICT, which processes kitchen waste (cooked and uncooked food waste) 
under mesophilic (35 ± 2 ◦C) conditions. To prepare FH, 1 kg of FW was 
mixed with 1 L of distilled water to form a slurry, which was homoge­
nized and passed through a mesh cloth to remove solids. The resultant 
filtrate was collected and used in co-digestion experiments to dilute PL.
2.1.1. Mixed microbial consortia and inoculum preparation
Mixed microbial consortia (MMC) were collected from an existing 
biogas plant based on an anaerobic gas lift reactor (AGR) operating at 
the Bowenpally vegetable market under mesophilic conditions (35 ±
2 ◦C) using vegetable waste as the substrate. The MMC was acclimatized 
with poultry PL for 7 days at mesophilic (35 ± 2◦C) temperature to serve 
as the inoculum for the study. After acclimatization, the inoculum was 
characterized for pH and VS which were found to be 7.1 and 6 %, 
respectively. Additionally, MMC containing SOB was isolated from a 
previous study, with detailed isolation procedures available in Bhavya 
et al. (2024). MMC-SOB was used in a 1:1 ratio in reactors labelled St-PL 
(10 %, 30 %, 60 %) to assess its effectiveness in inhibiting H2S 
production.
2.2. Experimental setup and operational procedures for poultry litter and 
food waste hydrolysate biomethanation
All SSAD batch experiments were conducted in 1 L glass reactors

equipped with arrangements for inlet, outlet, and biogas collection 
ports. Biogas generated from the SSAD reactors was continuously 
measured using the water displacement method over the 30-day 
experimental period. A total of 10 SSAD reactors were operated using 
PL and FH + PL at varying solids concentrations (10 %, 30 % and 60 %) 
at mesophilic temperature. Experimental details are summarized in 
Table 1. The initial pH of each reactor was adjusted to 7 ± 0.2 and 
sparged with N2 gas for 2 min to ensure anaerobic conditions. For re­
actors with stripping (St-PL at 10 %, 30 %, and 60 % solids concentra­
tions), daily 15 min of micro-aeration at a flowrate of 0.005 L/min was 
introduced into the reactor headspace to maintain partial aerobic con­
ditions for SOB activity. Rubber stoppers were used to seal the reactors 
tightly, with appropriate piping for gas collection and measurement. A 
substrate-to-inoculum (S/I) ratio of 1:1 was maintained across all re­
actors to balance microbial activity and substrate loading, minimizing 
lag phase and inhibition. All reactors were placed in an orbital shaker at 
70 rpm under mesophilic temperature conditions (35 ± 2 ◦C). Each 
experiment was performed in triplicate for consistency, and average 
values were used for calculations. Reactor pH was monitored every 
alternate day, while biogas production and methane content were ana­
lysed every two days. Samples (~5 g) were collected from each reactor 
every 10 days and analysed for TS, VS, COD, VFA, and ammoniacal 
nitrogen. Methane yield was calculated based on the VS remaining in the 
reactor. A standalone reactor was operated with MMC to estimate the 
biogas generation potential of the inoculum. The cumulative biogas 
generated by the inoculum was subtracted from the biogas generated in 
each experimental reactor to determine the net biogas production from 
PL.
2.3. Analytical parameters and procedures
The raw feed stock (i.e., PL) was initially characterized for TS, VS and 
moisture content (MC), VFA, Alkalinity using standard APHA 2005 
procedures (Baird et al., 2017). PL was also analysed for pH, alkalinity, 
chemical oxygen demand (COD), and ammoniacal nitrogen (A.N) by 
diluting the sample 10 times with DI water, as per APHA standard 
procedures (2005). Elemental analysis for carbon (C), hydrogen (H), 
nitrogen (N), and sulfur (S) was performed using a CHNS analyser 
(PerkinElmer, 2400 Series), with helium as the carrier gas and a thermal 
conductivity detector. Total volatile fatty acids (TVFAs) in the samples 
were determined using high-performance liquid chromatography 
(HPLC) (Shimadzu Model LC 10A VP) equipped with a UV detector (210 
nm) and ODS column (250 mm × 4.6 mm ID). A buffer solution of 0.01 
M H2SO4 in acetonitrile was used as the mobile phase at a flow rate of 
0.6 mL/min, with a sample injection volume of 20 µL. Gas chromatog­
raphy (GC) (Shimadzu GC-2010) was employed to analyse the biogas 
composition. The instrument was equipped with a thermal conductivity 
detector (TCD) and a Supelco Q Plot Biogas column (30 m × 0.53 mm). 
Nitrogen served as the carrier gas, with the column maintained at 38 ◦C, 
and detection and injection temperatures set at 250 ◦C and 200 ◦C, 
respectively. The injection volume was 1 mL. Heavy metals in the raw PL 
were quantified using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry 
(ICP-MS; model ICAP 6500 DUO). After the termination of the AD ex­
periments, the final digestate was analysed to evaluate its quality and 
suitability as an organic fertiliser (bio-manure). Parameters such as ni­
trogen (N), potash oxide (K2O), and phosphorus pentoxide (P2O5) were 
assessed in accordance with the Fertilizer Control Order (FCO) standards 
using ICP-MS. All analytical measurements were performed in triplicate 
to ensure accuracy, and the average values are reported. The chemicals 
used throughout the experiments were of analytical reagent grade.
2.4. Microbial community characterization using next generation 
sequencing
The raw PL collected from a local poultry farm, raw FH used for the 
experiments, and microbial sludge from the PL-30 %, PL + FH-30 %, and 
St + PL-30 % reactors three representative reactors with the highest 
performance in each category for sequencing, were collected on the 20th 
day when reactors reached steady- state methane production and stored 
at −20 ◦C in a 1:1 ethanol ratio to preserve samples for DNA isolation 
and subsequent characterisation, following the protocol outlined by 
Zhang et al. (2019a), Zhang et al. (2019b). The samples were gently 
thawed, and approximately 200 mg of each was used for DNA isolation, 
which was performed using the NucleoSpin® Soil Kit according to the 
manufacturer’s instructions (Roopnarain et al., 2017). The purity of the 
isolated DNA was quantified using the NanoDrop spectrophotometer 
method (Alessi et al., 2020). Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) was 
conducted to amplify the DNA isolated from the reactor samples for 
metagenomic studies aimed at understanding the diversity of bacterial 
species present in the reactors. A dual indexing PCR sequencing strategy 
was used to analyse the amplified DNA fragments on the Illumina 
sequencing platform. Amplicons were purified using the QIAGEN Puri­
fication Kit, and their purity and quantity were assessed with a Nano­
Drop method. The PCR cycling conditions included: an initial cycle at 
95 ◦C for 2 min, followed by 25 cycles of 95 ◦C for 15 s, 60 ◦C for 15 s, 
and 72 ◦C for 2 min, with a final extension at 72 ◦C for 10 min and a hold 
at 4 ◦C. Indexing primers targeting the V3-V4 variable region of the 16S 
rRNA bacterial gene (16S_F: 5′-AGAGTTTGATGMTGGCTCAG-3′; 16S_R: 
5′-TTACCGCGGCMGCSGGCAC-3′) were used to generate amplicon li­
braries. Following indexing PCR, the constructed libraries were quan­
tified using the Qubit fluorometer and the Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer 
system (Model 2939A). Sequencing of the enriched libraries was per­
formed at Biokart India using the Illumina HiSeq 2000 platform. The 
sequencing data obtained were analysed for alpha diversity (Chao1, PD 
whole tree, observed OTUs), which was calculated using R software. 
Beta diversity and taxonomic analysis were also performed. The sum­
mary of species diversity was examined using the QIIME platform, an 
advanced bioinformatics tool.
2.5. Statistical analysis
2.5.1. Kinetic study on the performance of solid-state anaerobic digestion 
reactors using three model equations
In this study, three kinetic models-the modified Gompertz model, the 
logistic model, and the transfer function model as shown in equations 
(Eq. 1, Eq. 2 and Eq. 3), were applied to fit experimental data on biogas 
production from PL. These models were used to evaluate the lag phase of 
the digestion process, predict the maximum biogas generation rate, and 
provide insights into the dynamics of biogas production.
Each kinetic model offered specific advantages. The modified Gom­
pertz model, widely recognised as an effective empirical non-linear 
regression model, was specifically employed to simulate methane

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Feedstock characterization and its significance in solid state 
anaerobic digestion
The characteristics of the substrate play a crucial role in determining 
its potential for biogas production. PL was found to be biodegradable 
with potential for biogas production. Numerous studies have identified 
PL as an excellent substrate, due to its high biodegradable content, 
which can be effectively harnessed for biofuel generation. A detailed 
summary of PL characteristics is provided in Table 2. The pH of PL was 
found to be 7.9, which is within the optimal range for AD. However, the 
VS/TS ratio (0.39) and C/N ratio (8.9) are relatively low, raising con­
cerns about microbial activity and process stability. To address this, co- 
digestion with FH was introduced. The VFA/alkalinity ratio of PL was 
1.4, indicating high VFA production. This necessitates careful pH 
monitoring to maintain the buffering capacity of the AD system. Stable 
mesophilic temperature and adequate retention time are critical for 
promoting methanogens to convert VFAs into methane effectively. The 
high ammoniacal nitrogen (1500 mg/L) and sulfate (5000 mg/L) con­
tent in PL present additional challenges. Ammonia inhibits metha­
nogens, which are more sensitive to its effects compared to acidogenic 
and acetogenic bacteria. Similarly, high sulfate levels lead to H2S pro­
duction by SRB, adversely impacting both the AD process and biogas 
quality. To mitigate these issues, an SOB consortium isolated from 
different sulfur rich sources and enriched with aerobic culture media 
(ACM) was introduced for desulfurisation in the AD reactors (St-PL at 10 
%, 30 %, and 60 % solids concentrations). The elemental composition of 
PL was determined to be 18.76 % carbon, 3.12 % hydrogen, 2.09 % 
nitrogen, and 1.42 % sulfur. Trace metal analysis showed cadmium, 
chromium, copper, lead, nickel, and zinc at 0.001 mg/L, 0.001 mg/L, 
0.084 mg/L, 0.033 mg/L, 0.006 mg/L, and 0.134 mg/L, respectively. 
Additionally, the COD, alkalinity, and VFA concentrations were found to 
be 140,000 mg/L, 4000 mg/L as CaCO3, and 5681 mg/L as CH3COOH, 
respectively (Table 2). Metagenomic studies were conducted to inves­
tigate the impact of microbial consortia on biogas generation and to 
examine shifts in bacterial diversity at different solids concentrations.
3.2. Impact of substrate solid concentration and co-digestion on methane 
yield and biogas generation potential
The AD experiments were conducted with PL at TS concentration of 
10 %, 30 % and 60 % in nine batch reactors along with one reactor 
containing food waste FH under mesophilic conditions (35 ± 2 ◦C). The 
reactors were designated as PL-10 %, PL-30 %, PL-60 %; PL + FH-10 %, 
PL + FH-30 %, PL + FH-60 %; St + PL-10 %, St + PL-30 %, St + PL-60 %, 
and FH. The daily biogas production and cumulative biogas yield over 
the 30-day experimental period are graphically represented in Fig. 1 (a) 
and (b). Peak biogas generation varied from 270 mL to 500 mL between 
days 14 and 16. The cumulative biogas and methane concentration were 
as follows: 5.9 L (47 % CH4), 9.9 L (49 % CH4), 5.39 L (45 % CH4), 11.5 L

that increasing the solids concentration in the reactor initially enhanced 
methane yield due to the greater availability of feedstock for microbial 
activity. However, at 60 % solids concentration, the digestion process 
was adversely affected, likely due to microbial inhibition from mass 
transfer limitations. The composition of PL at these solids concentration, 
combined with co-digestion, has limited studies available for direct 
comparison. However, comparable trends were observed in previous 
studies reported in literature. For instance, several researchers (Abbassi- 
Guendouz et al., 2012; Di Maria et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2016; Capson- 
Tojo et al., 2017) have observed that solids concentrations up to 25 % 
resulted in higher methane yield, whereas higher solids concentration 
were associated with reduced methane production. The experimental 
results from reactors with 30 % solids concentration, namely PL-30 %, 
PL + FH-30 %, and St + PL-30 %, demonstrated high performance in 
terms of both biogas generation and methane yield compared to other 
reactors.
The stability and operational mechanisms of the AD reactors were 
assessed by tracking key performance indicators such as alkalinity, VFA, 
TS, and VS, measured on the 10th, 20th, and 30th days. Additionally, pH 
was monitored at 2-day intervals. These results are illustrated in Fig. 2
(a-c). As shown in Fig. 2(a), the alkalinity levels in most reactors 
remained relatively stable. However, in the PL + FH 10 %, PL + FH 30 
%, and PL + FH 60 % reactors, showed a measurable decline in alka­
linity, consistent with the accumulation of VFAs during early-stage hy­
drolysis and acidogenesis processes occurring in these reactors.
This interpretation is further supported by the increased VFA levels 
in the PL + FH reactors, which followed trends similar to those seen in 
the other reactors. Fig. 2(b) shows the variation in pH across the re­
actors. The pH levels in the PL and St-PL reactors were stable, ranging 
from neutral to slightly basic. However, a gradual decrease in pH was 
observed in the PL-30 % reactor after 10 days. In contrast, the PL + FH 
reactors exhibited slightly acidic pH levels throughout the experiment, 
likely due to the accumulation of VFAs. The VFA profile, illustrated in 
Fig. 2(a), shows a notable increase in VFAs during the first 10 days, 
followed by a slight decline. The initial 10-day period was characterized 
by a reduction in pH, an increase in VFAs, and a decline in alkalinity, 
indicating the active presence of acidogenic and hydrolytic bacteria. The 
variation in the VFA was due to diversity of substrate fractions and 
biodegradability, persistence of VFAs after the methane plateau linked 
to residual hydrolysis and partial acid inhibition at higher solid load. 
Subsequently, the observed increase in pH, a slight reduction in VFAs, 
and a rise in alkalinity suggest the transition to methanogenesis as the 
dominant process within the reactors. Fig. 2(c) highlights the reduction 
in TS and VS levels across all reactors, except for the 60 % TS reactors. 
The reduced performance in the 60 % TS reactors can be attributed to 
the very high solids concentration, which likely impeded microbial ac­
tivity and mass transfer efficiency.
3.3. The effect of micro-aeration and sulfur oxidizing bacteria addition on 
H2S removal in biogas
The H2S levels in the biogas obtained from reactors labelled as St-PL 
(10 %, 30 %, 60 %) following the implementation of micro-aeration and 
SOB are illustrated in Fig. 3. In other reactors, daily H2S emission ranged 
from 0.2 % to 1.5 %, and these values were used as a baseline to 
determine the H2S removal efficiency in the St-PL reactors. The desul­
furization efficiency in the St-PL reactors ranged from 80 % to 92 %, as 
evident in Fig. 3. Although the H2S concentration decreased signifi­
cantly compared with the other reactors, complete removal of sulfide 
from the biogas was not achieved. The highest removal efficiency was 
observed in the St-PL-30 % reactor. H2S is a metabolic byproduct of SRB, 
and the observed reduction in cumulative H2S production in the St-PL 
reactors can be attributed to the inhibition of SRB activity. Previous 
studies have shown that low concentration of oxygen exerts toxic effects 
on SRB by generating reactive oxygen species and competing with sul­
fate as an electron acceptor. This interference inhibits dissimilatory 
sulfate reduction and may inactivate SRB (Brioukhanov & Netrusov, 
2007). The maximum desulfurisation efficiency achieved in this study 
was 92 %, which is notably higher than the values reported by Zhou 
et al. (2007). Conversely, the activity of SOB led to the conversion of 
gaseous H2S into sulfate or elemental sulfur in the digestate. As a result, 
the sulfate concentration in the digestate of St-PL reactors were consis­
tently higher than those in other reactors, as will be discussed in Section 
3.8. The reduction in H2S also increased the availability of methano­
genic substrates, likely enhancing methanogenic activity under micro- 
aerated conditions. Notably, the relative abundance of hydro­
genotrophic methanogens, particularly Methanocellus, increased signif­
icantly in the St-PL reactors, as elaborated in the subsequent section. The 
interplay between the activities of SRB and methanogens in utilising 
electron donors has been previously reported by Damianovic and Foresti 
(2009). The high sulfate concentrations observed in the St-PL reactors 
may also reflect sustained methanogenic activity, contributing to higher 
methane yields. In addition to achieving significant H2S removal, the 
introduction of micro-aeration and SOB consortia in the St-PL reactors 
resulted in a notable enhancement in methane production. This dual 
benefit underscores the effectiveness of this strategy in improving biogas 
quality and reactor performance.
Several studies have highlighted the significant impact of intro­
ducing small amounts of air or oxygen into AD processes on perfor­
mance. However, the level of enhancement observed in this study 
exceeded those reported previously, particularly in the St-PL 30 % 
reactor, which achieved the highest methane concentration of 68.2 %, 
compared to other reactors in this study, where methane concentrations 
ranged from 45 % to 61 %. For instance, Tsapekos et al. (2017)
demonstrated a 7.2 % increase in methane yield when 5 mL O2/g VS was 
introduced into an AD system processing wheat straw over three days. 
Similarly, Lim & Wang (2013) reported a 21 % improvement in methane 
production from brown water and food waste under micro-aeration 
(37.5 mL O2/L reactor/day for four days) compared with strictly 
anaerobic conditions. These findings, along with the results of the pre­
sent study, highlight the critical role of substrate characteristics in 
determining the effectiveness of micro-aeration strategies. PL, which is

Additionally, the degradation of substrates like PL leads to high levels of 
sulfur compounds, ammonia (NH3), and VFAs, creating conditions that 
promote H2S production and inhibit methanogenesis. The outcome and 
benefits of micro-aeration strategies are highly substrate-specific, with 
more pronounced effects observed in systems processing substrates like 
PL. This emphasizes the necessity of tailoring micro-aeration approaches 
to the unique characteristics of feedstock.
3.4. Effect of microbial consortia on the methanogenesis process: 
Microbial diversity in reactors
Metagenomic studies were conducted to analyse the microbial 
communities within the reactors. Five samples-PL-30 %, PL + FH 30 %, 
and St-PL 30 %, which demonstrated the highest biogas production and 
H2S removal efficiency-were selected for analysis. Additionally, raw PL 
and raw FH samples were included to compare microbial shifts between 
the raw substrates and reactor samples after digestion. The shifts in 
microbial community distribution at the phylum level are illustrated in 
Fig. 4. As shown in Fig. 4, the relative abundance of bacterial commu­
nities at the phylum level reveals substantial differences between the 
raw samples and reactor sludge samples. In all the AD reactors, Firmi­
cutes emerged as the most abundant bacterial phylum, accounting for 
43–70 % of total reads. This was followed by Bacteroidetes (30–36 %) 
and Actinobacteria (7–14 %). Other notable bacterial phyla included 
Chloroflexi (1–2 %), Spirochaetes (1–2 %), and Synergistetes (0.4–1 %), 
which are frequently reported in AD processes (Lee et al., 2016; Yin 
et al., 2018). Firmicutes play a key role in AD by breaking down complex 
organic substrates into intermediates such as H2, acetic acid, CO2, and 
butyric acid, while Bacteroidetes are active during hydrolysis and 
acidogenesis, degrading lipids and cellulose compounds, which en­
hances substrate availability and overall biogas production (Zhang et al., 
2019; Westerholm & Schnürer, 2019). Proteobacteria, another common 
hydrolytic bacterial group, utilise glucose, acetate, and propionate, and 
share metabolic pathways with Firmicutes during the acetogenesis phase. 
In addition to bacterial communities, archaeal communities play a sig­
nificant role in methane production, with their abundance varying 
across different stages of the AD process.
The microbial diversity results differed significantly in the St-PL 30 
% reactor due to the introduction of micro-aeration and the SOB con­
sortia. In this reactor, the relative abundance of Firmicutes, particularly 
the order Clostridiales, increased. Similarly, members of the Proteobac­
teria phylum showed a 32 % rise in relative abundance under the same 
conditions. Previous studies have noted that many SRB and SOB are 
classified under Proteobacteria, and the SOB consortia used in this 
reactor contained approximately 80 % Proteobacteria (Pokorna & Zab­
ranska, 2015; Bhavya et al., 2024).
The enhanced methane yield, faster hydrolysis kinetics, and 
maximum H2S suppression observed in the St-PL 30 % reactor suggest 
that differences in bacterial richness and diversity likely existed, even in 
the absence of significant variations in phyla proportions, as shown in 
Fig. 4. Additionally, the activity of bacterial populations may have 
shifted. For instance, under oxidative stress, the growth rate of ace­
togens has been reported to decrease significantly without impairing 
their acetate synthesis activity (Brioukhanov & Netrusov, 2007). The St- 
PL 30 % reactor demonstrated the highest biogas production and H2S 
suppression due to SOB activity. Micro-aeration likely facilitated an 
anaerobic micro-environment, where methanogens were shielded from 
oxidative stress primarily because of oxygen uptake by facultative bac­
teria within these phyla. These bacteria consumed oxygen, preventing it 
from directly harming methanogens and maintaining the local anaerobic 
conditions essential for methanogenic activity and biogas yield. This 
protective mechanism, critical to the success of the micro aeration 
strategy, relies on efficient oxygen utilisation by facultative bacteria, 
which create a “buffer zone” to ensure uninterrupted AD (Wanga et al., 
1999). In this study, different SRB, including Desulfovibrio, Desulfobulbus 
(Proteobacteria), and Desulfitibacter (Firmicutes), were found in the di­
gesters at relatively low abundances (<5%). Under micro-aerated con­
ditions, their abundance decreased by approximately half. These genera, 
commonly found in sulfate reduction reactors, are classified as incom­
plete organic oxidisers. Desulfobulbus and Desulfovibrio species are 
known to utilise ethanol, lactate, and hydrogen as electron donors, with 
sulfate serving as the electron acceptor, producing acetate as a 
byproduct (Liu et al., 2018). The decline in hydrogen-utilising SRB may 
have been offset by an increase in hydrogen-utilising methanogens. 
Conversely, several SOB, including Thioalkalimicrobium, Alishewanella, 
Bacillus (Firmicutes), and Pseudomonas (Proteobacteria), were detected in 
the St-PL 30 % reactor. These SOB likely contributed to the enhanced 
H2S removal efficiency by metabolising H2S and converting it into other 
sulfur compounds, such as sulfate or elemental sulfur, depending on the 
environmental conditions and metabolic pathways. Further details on 
the digestate composition are discussed in the subsequent section.
3.5. Comparison of archaeal community structures
Methanogens are the sole archaeal group responsible for converting 
organic matter into methane and carbon dioxide, a process carried out in 
symbiosis with bacteria. The presence and abundance of specific 
methanogenic archaea in AD systems directly influence the rate and 
efficiency of methanogenesis. The most abundant archaeal communities 
identified in the reactors were Methanosaeta and Methanobacterium, both 
belonging to the phylum Euryarchaeota. Methanomicrobia is considered 
key methanogens in AD system (Kumar Awasthi et al., 2021). The 
phylum Euryarchaeota utilises intermediate products such as acetate, H2, 
and CO2 as substrates to produce methane through various methano­
genic pathways. Metagenomic analysis of the reactor samples provided 
insights into the dominant methanogenic species and community shifts. 
The results revealed that Euryarchaeota was the predominant archaeal 
group in all reactors. Additionally, the presence of Crearchaeota and 
Parvarchaeota, both parts of the kingdom Archaea, was observed. 
Taxonomic analysis showed that Euryarchaeota accounted for 57 % of all 
archaeal organisms in the control reactor, increasing to 86 %, 84 %, and 
80 % in reactors St-PL 30 %, PL + FH 30 %, and PL 30 %, respectively. 
The biogas production data correlated with the highest abundance of 
Euryarchaeota in reactor St-PL 30 %, followed by PL + FH 30 % and PL 
30 %.
In raw PL and FH samples, Methanosaeta was the most dominant 
genus within Euryarchaeota, comprising 29–32 % of the archaeal com­
munity, followed by Methanoculleus (2–4 %), Methanosarcina (3–4 %), 
and Methanocorpusculum (2–4 %). Other methanogens, including

3.6. Kinetic potential parameters of anaerobic digestion
The kinetic analysis of AD of PL was performed by using three kinetic 
models: the modified Gompertz, logistic, and transfer function models. 
These models were utilized to estimate the hydrolysis rate constant, lag 
phase, maximum methane production rate, and maximum methane 
yield under mesophilic conditions, as summarised in Table 3. Experi­
mental biogas production from the reactors was compared with biogas 
yields predicted by these models. As shown in Fig. 6, the modified 
Gompertz, logistic, and transfer function models exhibited excellent 
agreement with the experimental data, with R2 values exceeding 0.96. 
Figs. 6(a) to 6(j) demonstrate the overlap between experimental and 
predicted values for all reactors, further corroborating the data pre­
sented in Table 3.
The lag phase for all reactors was calculated, with the longest lag 
phase observed in the PL + FH 60 % reactor across all models. This 
extended lag phase can be attributed to the high solid’s concentration of 
the substrate, which likely inhibited microbial activity. Among the three 
models, the modified Gompertz model provided the best fit for the 
experimental biogas yields (R2 = 0.99), with deviations remaining 
under 30 %, except for the FH reactor. While the logistic and transfer 
function models also performed well, the modified Gompertz model 
demonstrated superior accuracy in predicting biogas yields and lag 
phases.

Elevated levels of these metals, if present, could adversely affect plant

and more efficient biodigester management. To optimise the utilisation 
of PL, a cost-effective, environmentally sustainable, and labour-efficient 
method should be adopted. Considering the environmental challenges 
associated with odour, pathogen contamination, and greenhouse gas 
emissions, AD of PL represents a beneficial approach for renewable 
energy production and sustainable waste management.
4. Conclusions
This study demonstrated that SSAD of poultry litter at high solids 
concentrations (up to 30 % TS) correlates positively with biogas yield, 
achieving 0.31 L/gVSreduced (PL + FH 30 %), 0.28 L/gVSreduced (PL-30 
%), 0.3 L/gVSreduced (St-PL 30 %). The improved C/N ratio from 8.9 (PL) 
to 29.2 (PL + FH), contributed to the overall increase in biogas yield. 
The integration of SOB and micro-aeration effectively reduced H2S 
levels in the biogas, enhancing its suitability as a biofuel. Metagenomic 
analysis revealed that microbial diversity and composition were influ­
enced by solid concentrations and bioreactor parameters, highlighting 
their critical role in biogas generation efficiency. Additionally, the 
nutrient-rich digestate offers potential as a sustainable fertilizer alter­
native. Overall, the findings highlight the dual benefits of SSAD of 
poultry litter for efficient waste management and renewable energy 
production, offering a viable and sustainable approach to address
